A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same silence-bias study and AVH-Align method. All pages, including figures, tables, equations and references, support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original silence-bias measurements, detector evaluations, AVH-Align results and component ablations in Sections 3–4.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports additional dataset-bias analyses, SpeechForensics comparisons and AVLips evaluations.

M1.justification: Section 4.1 revises the reported scoring procedure: v1 defines fakeness through the complement of Eq. 2's alignment probability, whereas v2 specifies negative alignment scores before log-sum-exp pooling. The supervised formulation also introduces negated scores and explicit sigmoid conversion. The backbone, alignment MLP and unsupervised training objective remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained FakeAVCeleb and AV-Deepfake1M evaluations, v2 tests silence and volume biases on LAV-DF, AVLips and DFDC. It also evaluates AVH-Align and its ablations on AVLips, explicitly identified as independent of the VoxCeleb2 source dataset. This substantially broadens empirical coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds SpeechForensics to the unsupervised comparison. Table 3 removes the entire zero-shot group—Video-LLaMA, CLAP, M2TR, LipForensics, Face X-Ray and SBI—and the video-level Meso4, MesoInception and SBI comparisons. Segment-level and frame-level comparisons remain, so comparator coverage changes substantially.

E3.justification: The central trimming intervention changes from removing a fixed 40 ms from every clip to removing detected leading silence, using a 5 × 10^-4 threshold and rounding up to a video-frame boundary. v2 also adds average precision alongside AUC and reports score drops as AUC-point differences rather than relative percentages. These materially revise the robustness evaluation and metric reporting.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of bias generality across three datasets and contrasts FakeAVCeleb FVRA and RVFA subsets to investigate the role of synthesized audio. Section 4.5 extends existing component ablations to AVLips and tests whether the VoxCeleb2 pretraining advantage persists outside VoxCeleb2-derived evaluation data. Conversely, trimmed ablation results and three Figure 5 examples are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting; the table arrows indicate performance differences rather than statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Many AUC entries change across Tables 1, 2, 4 and 5. For example, Table 2 revises untrimmed FakeAVCeleb AVH-Align AUC from 96.3 to 94.6 and adds SpeechForensics at 98.8, exceeding AVH-Align there. AP results, AVLips ablation results and additional bias findings are new. Table 3 changes the silence classifier from 98.68 to 98.44. Revised scoring and trimming prevent interpreting these collectively as same-setting performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: Eq. 4 changes from CE(logsumexp(Phi_ii), y) to BCE(sigmoid(logsumexp(-Phi_ii)), y), revising the formal score-to-loss definition, including the sign inside pooling. Equations 1–3 are retained, and neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: leading-silence bias in two datasets, exploitation of that shortcut by detectors, and improved robustness through alignment learned from real data only. The additional evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting weaker biases to unchanged audio and the pretraining advantage to VoxCeleb2's larger size. Section 4.3 acknowledges a small trimming effect on AVH-Align and restricts its stated advantage over the compared unsupervised methods to AV-Deepfake1M. The broader discussion and recommendations remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, specifies 10,000 evaluation samples and the positive class, and clarifies that one AV-HuBERT model makes two forward passes. The newly disclosed sample count does not establish that the earlier count differed. Training budgets, learning rates and checkpoint information remain, while some MDS and AVAD architecture details are removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for DFDC, DiMoDif, SpeechForensics and AVLips, while removing the Face X-Ray, M2TR, CLAP and Video-LLaMA references associated with omitted comparisons. The related-work taxonomy and positioning relative to supervised and unsupervised detection remain largely intact.

P1.justification: The six-section narrative and most prose are retained. Changes include local grammar edits, rewritten scoring and experimental paragraphs, additional analysis paragraphs, reordered equal-contribution authors and new acknowledgments. There is no extensive narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: Table 2 is substantially restructured into AUC and AP blocks; Table 3 loses two comparison groups; and Table 4 replaces paired trimming columns with three dataset columns. Figure 5 retains nine of twelve example panels and is relocated. Figure 4 moves and gains explanatory caption text, while Figure 2's axes are rescaled. These materially revise the empirical displays.

improvement.justification: The additional bias checks and AVLips pretraining analysis provide evidence about the generality and possible confounds of the original findings. SpeechForensics, AP reporting and clearer implementation/access information also improve assessment of the work. These benefits outweigh the loss of some comparison and trimmed-ablation evidence, but broad superiority language remains despite SpeechForensics outperforming AVH-Align on FakeAVCeleb. The net improvement is limited.
